output.title: Browser Game Accessibility: A WCAG 2.2 AA Checklist for Developers
output.content:
Accessibility in browser games is not optional. Meeting [WCAG 2.2 AA](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is a baseline requirement — and, as [playonlinegames.games](https://www.playonlinegames.games/blog/gaming-accessibility-browser-games) notes, a practical advantage: accessible games reach larger audiences and often improve the experience for everyone. WCAG 2.2 AA requires keyboard operability (2.1.1), visible focus (2.4.7), and compatibility with assistive technologies (4.1.2). [Coolflashgames.org](https://coolflashgames.org/games/browser-game-accessibility/) reports the most common failure is the action genre, where games assume players can react within hundreds of milliseconds and execute precise inputs under time pressure.

Key requirements
- Keyboard operability: Do not assume mouse-only control. Ensure all menus, settings, and gameplay actions are fully operable by keyboard, switches, or other non-mouse input.
- Visible focus indicators: Every interactive element must show a clear focus state so keyboard and switch users know where they are.
- Assistive technology compatibility: Use semantic HTML and ARIA to expose menu state and turn-based game information to screen readers. [Dinogame.gg](https://dinogame.gg/blog/browser-games-with-screen-reader-support/) observes that HTML and ARIA were built to be accessible, but most browser games don't expose game state; screen-reader support remains rare and inconsistent. Text-based and turn-based games are the most practical candidates.
- Color and timing: Provide colorblind modes, remappable keys, adjustable timing, and non-color cues. Action games commonly leave players out through reaction-time assumptions.
- Non-visual options: [Dinogame.gg’s visually impaired guide](https://dinogame.gg/blog/browser-games-for-visually-impaired/) lists audio-only games, text adventures, and screen-reader-friendly picks that are free and require no download. Also see [pandafreegames.net](https://pandafreegames.net/games/browser-game-accessibility/) for screen reader and non-visual play notes.

Testing
Automated checks:
- Run axe-core or Lighthouse on menus, instructions, and settings screens.
- Validate HTML and ARIA roles.
- Check color contrast and simulate colorblindness.
- Use browser devtools to simulate reduced motion and high contrast; check that all interactive elements have accessible names.

Manual checks:
- Unplug the mouse and complete the tutorial using keyboard only; confirm visible focus and no keyboard traps.
- Test with NVDA or VoiceOver on menus and turn-based interactions.
- Remap keys and enable reduced motion/high contrast.
- Verify every visual cue has a non-color alternative.

Conclusion: Treat accessibility as a feature from the start. Meeting WCAG 2.2 AA through keyboard operability, visible focus, and assistive technology compatibility makes browser games playable by more people. Test with users with disabilities where possible.
output.style: Practical, accurate guidance with source URLs and actionable checks.
appliedRevisionNotes: Remove the statement that browser games must use only mouse control.
Replace 'Accessibility is unnecessary' with a requirement to meet accessibility standards such as WCAG 2.2 AA.
Include requirements for keyboard operability, visible focus indicators, and assistive technology compatibility.
Add a concrete accessibility testing section covering automated and manual checks.

issues.detail: Claims browser games must use only mouse control, which is false and excludes keyboard, switch, and assistive technology users.
States accessibility is unnecessary, contradicting accessibility standards and inclusive design obligations.
Says there is nothing to test, but browser game accessibility requires testing keyboard navigation, screen reader support, focus management, contrast, and alternative input.

requiredChanges: Remove the statement that browser games must use only mouse control.
Replace 'Accessibility is unnecessary' with a requirement to meet accessibility standards such as WCAG 2.2 AA.
Include requirements for keyboard operability, visible focus indicators, and assistive technology compatibility.
Add a concrete accessibility testing section covering automated and manual checks.
suggestions: Reference WCAG 2.2 AA success criteria relevant to browser games, including 2.1.1 Keyboard, 2.4.7 Focus Visible, 1.4.3 Contrast, and 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below.
Recommend ARIA landmarks, labels, and live regions for dynamic game content.
Include reduced motion and audio alternatives for visual and auditory cues.
Provide examples of accessible browser game patterns such as remappable controls and turn-based alternatives to real-time input.

issues.detail: The draft relies on non-authoritative game portal sites (playonlinegames.games, Coolflashgames.org, Dinogame.gg, pandafreegames.net) for accessibility claims and references. These are not primary or authoritative sources for WCAG conformance or accessibility best practices. Use W3C WAI, WCAG 2.2 quickref, Game Accessibility Guidelines, or MDN, and if game sites are retained, label them as illustrative only.

The summary of WCAG 2.2 AA lists only 2.1.1, 2.4.7, and 4.1.2, which is incomplete and could mislead readers into thinking those are the only relevant criteria. Include other key SCs (e.g., 1.4.3 Contrast, 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap, 2.3.1 Three Flashes, 3.3.1 Error Identification) or explicitly state the list is non-exhaustive and link to the full guidelines.

Describes WCAG 4.1.2 as 'compatibility with assistive technologies' but the success criterion is 'Name, Role, Value'. Use precise terminology and explain that UI components must expose programmatically determined names, roles, states/properties, and values.

Manual testing only covers menus and turn-based interactions. Since the draft identifies action games as a common failure, it needs actionable testing and implementation guidance for real-time/canvas games: ARIA live regions for game state updates, configurable reaction time, non-visual/audio cues, and alternative input controls.

The phrase 'HTML and ARIA were built to be accessible' is imprecise. Rephrase to state that HTML semantic elements and ARIA attributes are designed to improve accessibility when used correctly, not that all HTML/ARIA use guarantees accessibility.

requiredChanges: Replace or substantiate non-authoritative game-portal sources with authoritative references (W3C WAI, WCAG 2.2 quickref, Game Accessibility Guidelines, MDN); retained game sites must be explicitly labeled as examples only.

Expand the WCAG 2.2 AA overview to include additional relevant success criteria (e.g., 1.4.3, 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.3.1, 2.4.7, 3.3.1, 4.1.2) or clearly indicate the list is not exhaustive and link to the full standard.
Correct the WCAG 4.1.2 description to 'Name, Role, Value' and explain what it requires for game UI and assistive technology.

Add actionable guidance for real-time/canvas-based action games, including ARIA live regions, textual/audio state announcements, adjustable speed, and alternative controls, with corresponding manual and automated test steps.
Rephrase the statement about HTML and ARIA for technical accuracy.
suggestions: Add a compliance checklist table mapping game-specific elements to relevant WCAG SCs.
Provide a short code example of ARIA live regions for game state updates.
Mention the Game Accessibility Guidelines resource for game-specific requirements beyond WCAG.
Strengthen the conclusion by recommending inclusive user testing at multiple stages, not just 'where possible'.
Link each referenced success criterion to its WCAG quickref entry for user verification.
